title: The internet crosses oceans on cables, not satellites
description: Over 99% of intercontinental data travels through cables on the seabed. Here is how light and electricity make that work.

scenes.say: You might think satellites carry the internet across oceans. They don't. Submarine cables carry over ninety-nine percent of intercontinental data.

steps: Landing station hands it to land
scenes.say: Inside each cable are optical fibers. Your data is turned into flashes of light that race through glass. Over thousands of kilometers, the light fades, so repeaters along the cable boost it.
Those repeaters sit on the seabed, far from any plug. So power is fed from the landing stations on shore, as a steady direct current running along the cable itself.
And the cable is thin. Typically just seventeen or twenty-four millimeters across. Wider means more expensive, which limits how many fibers fit inside, and how much power can be shared.
So the next time you stream something from another continent, thank a cable on the ocean floor. Follow for more of how the internet really works.
